newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Honeywell sees strong EPS growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Honeywell sees strong EPS growth.

text.p: Honeywell Inc, reporting 21-percent earnings growth in 1996 and a strong order backlog, looks for more double-digit growth this year, chief financial officer William Hjerpe told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"We're getting good top-line growth and good margin expansion in every one of our business segments," Hjerpe said, adding, "We've committed ourselves to solid double-digit earnings per share increases."
Hjerpe said this is in keeping with a three-year strategy outlined by the company in late 1994.

The Minneapolis-based controls company posted earnings per share increases of 22 percent in 1995 and 21 percent in 1996, and Hjerpe expects "another solid year of earnings growth in 1997." He backed a $3.63 a share consensus estimate for 1997.
Cowen & Co analyst Jeffrey Sprague said Honeywell's $3.18 a share 1996 earnings surpassed expectations. He said its strong order bookings "set the stage for a very good 1997."
Honeywell has targeted a one- to two-point margin-rate expansion. Hjerpe said, "We're well within the committed range, having grown one-third point in 1995, one-half point in 1996."

Hjerpe expects margins to grow by one-third to one-half point this year. "And we're on track to achieve free cash flow generation of $900 million to $1 billion," over the three years that began in 1995, he said. In 1995 and 1996, about $620 million was generated in free cash flow, which is defined as cash from operations less capital expenditures.
Honeywell recorded 13 percent order growth in 1996 -- nine percent in home and building controls, 22 percent in the industrial sector and 17 percent in space and aviation.
"Growth is broadly based. Going into 1997 there's no one program or customer win on which we would be dependent," Hjerpe noted.
He said Honeywell's capital spending this year will be in a range of $250 million to $280 million. In 1996, it spent about $290 million.

Hjerpe also said he expects the company's board next week to approve another share repurchase program, "at the $250 million level." In 1996, the company bought back $163.2 million of stock, or 2.9 million shares. Hjerpe said the expected $250 million authorization would be "on top of about $38 million remaining" from the previous buyback program.
Honeywell was trading at 68, up one.
